query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (approximately 0.3–0.5 wt%) of niobium (Nb) to (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will promote grain boundary segregation and the formation of fine, ductile Nb-rich precipitates that blunt crack tips and impede crack propagation, thereby increasing the alloy’s load‐bearing integrity while preserving its caloric performance.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 as cast/annealed high-entropy alloy exhibiting a strong caloric response but with poor load-bearing integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.conditions: Operational conditions typical for solid refrigeration devices, including applied magnetic/pressure fields and temperature cycling near the caloric phase transition, with typical loading boundaries encountered in device operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nb segregates to grain boundaries and forms fine, ductile Nb-rich precipitates that lead to grain refinement and improved crack blunting.
generation.mechanism: The Nb-rich precipitates and segregation at grain boundaries reduce crack initiation and propagation by effectively blunting crack tips without disrupting the cooperative phase transition responsible for the magneto- and barocaloric effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved load-bearing integrity demonstrated by enhanced fracture toughness and ductility, while the magnitude and operational boundaries (field, pressure, temperature) of the caloric response remain statistically unchanged compared to the unchanged alloy.
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits large caloric effects under cyclic applied fields but suffers from cracking and poor mechanical reliability.
generation.boundary: The intervention should maintain performance within the operating regimes of applied magnetic and pressure fields and the temperature ranges typical for refrigeration, without introducing new phase transitions or shifting the caloric phase transition outside these limits.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact influence of Nb addition on the caloric transition parameters; careful tuning of the Nb concentration and heat-treatment process is required to ensure that the caloric performance is not compromised.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples, one with the addition of 0.3–0.5 wt% Nb and one without modification. Subject both sets to identical heat treatments and process conditions. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/TEM to confirm grain refinement and the presence of fine Nb-rich precipitates. Perform mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness, tensile strength) to assess improvements in load-bearing integrity, and measure the caloric response (magnitude and transition parameters) under applied magnetic and pressure fields across the relevant temperature range.
measurements: Grain size and precipitation analysis via SEM/TEM and possibly X-ray diffraction.
Fracture toughness and tensile tests to quantify improvements in load-bearing integrity.
Caloric effect measurements (e.g., magnetocaloric/barocaloric tests) under controlled field and temperature cycling.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-microalloyed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical integrity (e.g., fracture toughness, ductility) compared to the baseline alloy, or if the caloric response (magnitude or operating boundaries) is degraded or shifted outside the refrigeration application range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 5 schematically illustrates how a strong, ductile and stable material is created by combining alloying effect and scaling laws. In contrast to the strength-ductility trade-off for a bulk coarse-grained W and HEA, both strength and ductility are significantly improved in nanocrystalline HEA micropillars, compared with a bulk HEA, benefiting from reduced sample size and grain refinement (Fig. 5a). With regards to strength-stability synergy (Fig. 5b), the drawback of thermal instability in nanocrystalline W can be overcome by alloying in nanocrystalline HEAs that also results a higher strength level. Technologically, the fabrication and properties of this new class of small-dimension refractory HEAs are interesting and attractive. Although co-sputtering technique has been suggested to produce HEA films in some earlier reports,, to our knowledge this work constitutes the first report of the formation of single-phase nanostructured refractory HEAs. Furthermore, the fabrication process for these thin films is fast and controllable: the alloy composition, film thickness and grain size can be tuned.

While the yield strength and KJIc fracture toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi and high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloys are comparable, the tensile strengths, tensile ductility and work of fracture of the CrCoNi alloy are significantly higher, by respectively ∼15, ∼30 and ∼50%, at room temperature. At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths of the two alloys are comparable (σUTS∼1,300 MPa at 77 K), but the KJIc fracture toughness, tensile ductility and work of fracture are again markedly higher in the CrCoNi alloy, by ∼25, ∼27 and ∼31%, respectively. The yield strength, σy, at 77 K is slightly below that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which we believe is due to the non-uniform grain size of our present material (Fig. 1b–d). Consistent with this notion, in a previous study where the grain size of CrCoNi was uniform and comparable to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, the tensile properties of the three-component alloy were found to exceed those of the five-component alloy at all temperatures.

Strength and ductility (and hence toughness) are key mechanical properties of structural materials, although these properties are often mutually exclusive. In crystalline metallic materials, strength and ductility depend on the presence of crystal defects and how they move under mechanical loading. Dislocations serve as the prime carrier of plasticity in metals and their motion to create plastic deformation is strongly influenced by interactions with other dislocations as well as defects such as solute atoms, stacking faults, grain boundaries (GBs) and reinforcement particles or precipitates. In general, strong interactions (obstacles) strengthen a material although this often limits its ability to plastically deform. Twinning, however, appears to be a deformation mechanism capable of defeating this ‘conflict' between strength and ductility. The presence of twins usually serves to impede dislocation motion and induce strengthening, but multiple twinning systems can also enhance ductility. frame.system: The high‐entropy alloy (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 in its as‐cast/annealed state is a single‐phase or near single‐phase material that exhibits a large caloric (magneto‐/barocaloric) response under applied field and pressure but suffers from poor load‐bearing integrity with a tendency to crack.
frame.goal: Improve the alloy’s mechanical integrity (i.e. resistance to crack initiation and propagation under load) while preserving the exceptional caloric response under the operating magnetic/pressure fields and temperature ranges used in refrigeration.
frame.limitation: The alloy’s inherent brittleness, manifested as poor load‐bearing integrity and its predisposition to cracking, which limits its structural reliability in working devices despite its advantageous caloric properties.
constraints: Only a single intervention is allowed (i.e. one change in processing or composition)
The caloric performance (magnitude of the caloric effect under applied field and pressure) must be preserved
The intervention must be applicable within the operating field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries typical for solid refrigeration devices
frame.regime: The alloy is employed under operational conditions where magnetic and/or pressure fields are cyclically applied at temperatures near its caloric transition. The intervention must be effective under these same field and loading conditions (typical refrigeration operating pressures and fields, and thermal cycling in a moderate temperature range).
prior_attempts: No explicit previous interventions are mentioned, but the base alloy has been used as-is with high caloric response yet insufficient mechanical reliability, suggesting that previous efforts (if any) have not simultaneously improved integrity without degrading its caloric properties.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis seeks to improve a specific property (mechanical integrity) via a targeted microstructural modification while maintaining a second functional property (caloric performance). This requires an understanding of how minor compositional adjustments can promote desirable microstructural features (e.g. grain boundary strengthening, precipitation of ductile secondary phases) without interfering with the mechanism of the caloric effect (such as preserving the cooperative phase transition behavior).
frame.hypothesis: A single intervention that could address this is the microalloying of the base high‐entropy alloy with a small quantity (e.g., 0.3–0.5 wt%) of niobium (Nb). The proposed mechanism is that Nb will segregate at grain boundaries during solidification and subsequent heat treatments, promoting grain refinement and forming fine, ductile Nb-rich precipitates that act to blunt crack tips and impede crack propagation. This should enhance the load-bearing integrity (i.e., improve toughness and ductility) while minimally affecting the caloric (magneto-/barocaloric) phase transition responsible for refrigerant performance. The intervention is expected to maintain the critical field, pressure, and temperature boundaries under which the caloric effect is activated. Prior evidence from similar high-entropy and multi-component alloys indicates that microalloying with elements such as Nb can improve mechanical properties without degrading functional performance if the additional phases are sufficiently fine and well-distributed. A controlled experiment to test this hypothesis would compare samples of the original and Nb-modified alloy via: (a) microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) showing grain refinement and presence of Nb-rich precipitates; (b) mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness and tensile tests) demonstrating improved load-bearing integrity; and (c) caloric measurements (under identical magnetic/pressure fields and cycling temperatures) showing that the magnitude and reversibility of the caloric effect remain statistically unaltered. Should the Nb-added alloy either show degradation in the caloric response (or shift the transition parameters outside the desired operating regime) or fail to exhibit a significant improvement in mechanical integrity, the hypothesis would be falsified.

families.principle: Altering the alloy’s composition to subtly modify phase equilibria and segregation behavior, thereby promoting fine, ductile precipitates or beneficial grain boundary segregation while ideally leaving the caloric phase transition unaffected.
cues_against: risk that any compositional change might disrupt the precise conditions for the caloric phase transition
families.best_lever: Microalloying with a small amount (e.g., 0.3–0.5 wt%) of niobium (Nb) to induce grain boundary segregation and form fine, ductile precipitates.

families.principle: Engineering the internal microstructural features (grain size, grain boundary character, precipitate distribution) to blunt crack tips and impede crack propagation while preserving phase uniformity.
cues_for: proposed mechanism involves grain refinement and the formation of ductile precipitates at grain boundaries
need to improve load-bearing integrity without disturbing bulk caloric properties
cues_against: requires careful control to avoid altering the cooperative transition underlying the caloric effect
families.best_lever: Tailoring the microstructure through targeted alloying (e.g., Nb addition) that induces beneficial grain boundary segregation and ultrafine precipitate formation.

families.principle: Using post-solidification heat treatments or thermomechanical processing to induce controlled precipitation and grain refinement, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity.
cues_for: ability to tune precipitate formation and refine grain structure
cues_against: complex treatments might shift or broaden the caloric transition
risk that additional thermal cycles disturb the functional caloric regime
families.best_lever: A precisely controlled aging treatment designed to precipitate fine, ductile phases (such as Nb-rich precipitates if Nb is present) without interfering with the caloric phase transition.

families.principle: Modifying the processing conditions (e.g., casting, solidification rate) to control the microstructure, grain size, and defect population in the alloy, potentially enhancing mechanical toughness.
cues_for: intrinsic brittleness may be linked to processing routes
cues_against: altered processing could inadvertently modify the phase transition responsible for the caloric effect
risk of residual stresses or inhomogeneities affecting caloric performance
families.best_lever: Adjusting the cooling rate during solidification (e.g., rapid solidification) to achieve a finer, more homogeneous grain structure.

families.principle: Modifying the material’s surfaces or interfacial boundaries to enhance fracture toughness by mitigating stress concentration, potentially through coatings or localized treatments.
cues_for: grain boundary engineering is mentioned as a mechanism to impede crack propagation
cues_against: surface modifications typically affect only the near-surface region and might not address bulk mechanical integrity
the intervention is required to be a single change that works under operational (bulk) conditions
families.best_lever: Applying a thin, ductile coating that could shield the surface against crack initiation; however, this is less promising given the bulk nature of the integrity issues.
